name: Akhal-Teke
notes: Metallic / iridescent coat sheen - not modelled (a shader, out of scope).
NNF: an early-lethal foal disorder with no gene yet - see roadmap.

name: American Cream Draft
notes: Pale gold coat, amber eyes, pink freckled skin: gold champagne (Ch on a chestnut), not the cream dilution, which the breed does not carry.
EMS / laminitis: age-related, folded into heartiness.

The only draught breed developed in the United States, and traced to one cream foundation mare - Old Granny, foaled about 1911 - with the association formed in 1944. The Livestock Conservancy rates it Critical and the registered population is in the hundreds; it ships as rare here, which is a gameplay call rather than a reading of that status.

The real association test panel is exactly two loci, and both are clear here. PSSM1 (GYS1) ships as a gene but is not named: presence in the breed is documented and no population frequency is, and a dominant would show on every copy. JEB1 - junctional epidermolysis bullosa, a recessive lethal - has no locus in this mod at all; it is on the roadmap, and is deliberately not stood in for by an unrelated recessive lethal.
Champagne here is the real SLC36A1 dominant, and every founder carries a copy: the coat, the amber eye and the pink freckled skin all come off that one locus.

name: American Miniature
notes: Under 9.5 hh: the magic-size band bottoms this near the MAGICAL_MIN_SCALE guard - about as small as the model goes.
Dwarfism, dental overcrowding, EMS: ACAN dwarfism already exists; the rest fold into heartiness.

name: American Paint
notes: Pinto spotting: tobiano + sabino + frame overo + splash, all present. O/O (lethal white) is the real breeding hazard.
HYPP, HERDA and PSSM1 all have loci now - see SCN4A, PPIB and GYS1. HYPP is the breeding hazard here alongside O/O.

name: Anadolu
notes: A Turkish village landrace, not a closed show breed - bay, brown, black and chestnut are the core, with grey and true dun as real minorities.
No dilution, no pinto and no leopard: ancient Anatolian coat diversity is archaeology, not a modern founder pool.
All disorders clear - the Turkish screening data that exists is for Arabians, which is not evidence about this landrace.

name: Andalusian
notes: Thick flowing mane and tail, baroque compact build - mane length is a roadmap render item.
OCD, laminitis: age-related, folded into heartiness.

name: Anglo-Arabian
description: Arabian endurance crossed onto Thoroughbred scope, fixed as a breed of its own in France. Tall, rangy and grey more often than not.
notes: No dilution, no tobiano, no leopard complex - both parent breeds are base-colour-and-grey populations, so a patterned Anglo comes from outcrossing.
SCID, CA and LFS carry at Arabian-line rates; the studies behind them are of Arabians, not of Anglos.
Pedigree fractions are the real registry's definition of the breed and are not modelled - an Arabian bred to a Thoroughbred here makes a cross, not an Anglo-Arabian.
Dished face, stride length and endurance metabolism not modelled.

name: Appaloosa
notes: ERU (equine recurrent uveitis) is age-related; folded into heartiness. CSNB on LP/LP is modelled (informational).

name: Arabian
notes: Dished face and high-carried tail - head profile is not modelled; tail carriage could be a pose tweak (roadmap).
SCID, CA, LFS: early-lethal foal disorders - carried at the wild rate (PRKDC, TOE1, MYO5A).

name: Australian Stock Horse
description: Australia's working stock horse: compact, sure-footed and level-headed around cattle. Every colour is allowed, and it shows.
notes: "All colours" is the breed standard, so the pool is unusually wide - but solids stay the majority and a loud pinto is meant to be an outlier, not the look of the herd.
No leopard complex: Appaloosa blood is not part of the breed's description.

The four disorder rates are deliberately below the Quarter Horse figures they are borrowed from - there is no published Stock Horse panel survey, and the breed only has stock-horse ancestry in some modern lines.
Cow sense, campdrafting and the sure-footed walk are the breed's actual selling points and none of them are modelled.

name: Azteca
description: Mexico's own horse, made in 1972 from Iberian stock and Quarter Horses. Compact, powerfully built, and usually a solid dark colour or grey.
notes: Two strains, because the two registries disagree about what an Azteca may look like: nine founders in ten are the Mexican solid-coloured standard, one in ten carries the American registry's permitted Paint-derived patterns.
No leopard complex in either strain - the Mexican standard explicitly refuses Appaloosa patterning.

The disorder rates are Quarter Horse-derived risks kept deliberately low. The American registry requires breeding stock to test clear for all of them, which is evidence the loci matter to the breed, not evidence of a carrier rate.
Malignant hyperthermia (RYR1) is the fifth locus that registry screens, and this mod has no gene for it.

Foundation-blood percentages, registry inspection and charro training are what actually define the breed, and none of them are modelled: a Quarter Horse bred to an Andalusian here makes a cross, not an Azteca.

name: Baise Horse
notes: The Baise horse of the Baise region of Guangxi, in southwestern China. Filed here under its proper breed name rather than as a generic 'Guangxi horse' - Guangxi is the autonomous region, and the Debao Pony and the Guoxia come from the same ground.

Not one of China's big northern steppe horses: a compact southern mountain and village type, pony-sized but not refined - broad-jawed, dense-boned, short-legged, and built to carry people and supplies on narrow paths and pull a light cart.
Bronze horses from the third to first centuries BCE found in the region resemble the modern type closely. That is suggestive rather than proof of genetic continuity.
Four documented colours and no more: bay leads, with chestnut, black and grey as minorities. No population genotype survey exists for this breed, so the rates are transparent gameplay approximations.
The grey here is true progressive grey - born pigmented and lightening with age - and not silver dapple, not mouse dun and not a horse white from birth.

Every dilution, every white pattern and the whole leopard complex are forced wild. Ordinary face and lower-leg markings do occur on individuals, but the mod's named white loci all paint far more than that, and there is no evidence to hang them on.

Heat tolerant near-fixed: exceptional heat and humidity tolerance is the breed's documented adaptation, along with thrift on poor-to-medium forage and hard small hooves. Health 10 is that thrift; no cold locus.
All disorders clear. Real-world resilience to climate and forage is not evidence about any particular Mendelian allele, and no Baise-specific carrier frequency was located for any of them.
Genomic work identifies it as a distinctive Chinese indigenous population, protected regionally as an animal genetic resource. Traditional wedding use is noted in the sources.
The hard hooves, the forage efficiency and the narrow mountain-track sure-footedness are none of them modelled.

name: Banker Horse
notes: Primitive markings, Spanish-type head. Feral Colonial Spanish stock - hardy, few genetic issues.

name: Barb
notes: Grey-dominant by design: about seven founders in ten grey out, over a bay, black or chestnut base. Nothing else varies.
No dilution, no pinto, no roan, no leopard - the traditional palette is bay, black, chestnut and grey, and small face and leg white is not a named locus here.
All disorders clear. The one MENA study that found SCID found it in Arabians and a single Arab-Barb, which is not a pure-Barb rate.
Hard feet, heat tolerance and recovery after work - not modelled beyond heartiness and the heat-tolerance locus.

name: American Bashkir Curly
description: A rare, hardy North American saddle horse whose whole identity is the curl of its coat rather than its colour - so it comes in every colour there is.
notes: The curly coat is not modelled, and it is the entire breed. There is no hair-texture locus: KRT25 (curls with hair loss) and SP6 (curls without it) both exist in real Curlies, KRT25 is epistatic to SP6 for the hair loss, and this mod has neither gene - so a Bashkir Curly here is a hardy, eclectically coloured saddle horse and nothing on it is curly.
The two strains the breed really has are strains of curl, so they are not written here: with no curly locus they would be two identical empty strains.
The wide colour pool is the point - chestnut is the commonest, but bay, black, grey, every dilution, roan, pinto and leopard all occur, so a herd should look assorted.
CA carries at the 2.8% figure reported for the breed. HYPP and PSSM1 are kept very low and are borrowed from stock-horse lines rather than measured here.
Curl tightness, seasonal shedding, mane and ear curl, and the breed's reputation for suiting some allergic riders are all outside what the mod models.

name: Belgian Draft
notes: Flaxen mane and tail on a chestnut body, heavy muscling - the muscling reads through MSTN.
CPL, EMS, anhidrosis: age-related, folded into heartiness.

name: Boerperd
notes: The SA Boerperd - a Cape-derived farmer's horse. Broad in solid colour: bay, brown, black, chestnut, buckskin, palomino, smoky black, grey, roan and rare dun, with flaxen and rabicano as modifiers.
Solid-bodied by breed standard, which requires pigmented skin and rejects pinto-like marking - so tobiano, frame, splash, sabino and the W series are all absent.
Most are naturally five-gaited, with a rack or amble on top of the ordinary gaits. DMRT3 carries the gait allele, but gait itself is not modelled - see the roadmap.
All disorders clear: the breed has a performance-trait study but no carrier rates for this panel.
The distinction between SA Boerperd and Cape Boerperd is not modelled.

A double-cream foal is barred from registration, and breeders are warned off mating two cream dilutes. Cream is kept where it is - high enough for buckskin, palomino and smoky black, low enough that a double dilute is an uncommon founder - and the pair stays reachable by breeding, because it is a registry rule rather than a disorder. The same shape as the Chilean Corralero.

Traced to the Cape settlement after 1652, from Barb and Arabian-type horses imported by way of Java, and rebuilt from remote survivors after heavy losses in the Anglo-Boer wars. Mares must stand at least 13.3 hh and stallions at least 14.2 hh; the band here starts at 14.2 hh, so it is the stallion minimum that sets the floor and the smallest registrable mares fall below anything this breed rolls.
Black pigmented skin is required by the standard, which is the other half of why no white pattern is named here.

name: Budyonny
notes: Don mares on Thoroughbred stallions, rebuilt as Soviet cavalry remounts in the Rostov region and recognised in 1949. Four founders in five are chestnut; the rest are bay or brown, and black is scarce.
No wild herds - it is a state-stud and sport-horse breed, so the cowboy, the stables and the egg are the only ways to one.
The prized golden metallic sheen is coat quality, not a dilution, and is not modelled - the same loss as the Akhal-Teke and the Karabakh.

The three historical types - Massive, Eastern and Middle - are not strains here: a strain may override gene pools and nothing else, and the three differ only in conformation and size. The size band spans all three.
All disorders clear. Don, Thoroughbred and Arabian ancestry does not license importing their carrier rates.

name: Camargue
notes: Born dark, greys out to white; thick mop-like mane and tail. Melanoma is age-related (folded into heartiness).

name: Canadian Horse
notes: Dense thick mane and tail, 'little iron horse' build. Famously sound.

name: Caspian Pony
notes: Small, fine-boned, short legs, prominent eyes. 'Fragile bones' left as low heartiness rather than a lethal gene.

name: Chilean Corralero
notes: The Caballo de Pura Raza Chilena - the huaso's cattle horse, and the oldest registered native breed in South America (studbook 1893, closed 1934).
Dark and solid by preference: bay, dark bay and black lead, chestnut is a minority, and buckskin, palomino, dun, grey and roan all occur at low rates.

The real standard bars total or partial white and washed-out cream coats. Cream is kept low enough that a double-cream founder is very uncommon, but the pair is reachable by breeding - that is a registry rule, not a disorder.
Solid-bodied: no tobiano, frame, splash or leopard. Sabino is light, for ordinary face and leg white only.
All disorders clear - no Chilean-specific carrier data, and Quarter Horse, Arabian or warmblood rates are not a substitute.
Cow sense, the medialuna, thick skin, wavy mane and black concave hooves - none modelled.

name: Chincoteague Pony
description: A small, weatherproof salt-marsh pony off a barrier island, and the most reliably pinto thing running wild. Blue eyes are common.
notes: Tobiano is the signature and splash is the reason for the eyes - a herd should read as pinto ponies from a distance, with blue and part-blue eyes turning up far more often than in a feral population.

Two strains: eight founders in ten are the stocky island type, two in ten the taller privately-bred sport type. The sport type should also be the larger of the two and is not, because a strain can override gene pools but not the stats block.

ACAN D5 dwarfism is tested for in the real breed and is not here: this mod's ACAN gene declares D1 to D4, and D1 is the severe one, so borrowing a different variant's allele would overstate what it does.

The association's other listed risks - uveitis, lordosis, EMS, laminitis, DSLD, CIAR - are mostly not single-gene conditions and have no locus here. They are deliberately not stood in for by unrelated disorders.
Salt tolerance, marsh grazing, the dense winter coat, swimming and the pony penning are all outside what the mod models.

name: Cleveland Bay
notes: Always bay with black points, minimal white. Fixed A_ plus an E-heavy extension keeps it off chestnut and black.

name: Clydesdale
notes: Heavy lower-leg feathering - roadmap render layer. Sabino + splash drive the big white legs and face.
CPL, sunburn: age-related, folded into heartiness.

name: Colorado Ranger
notes: A pedigree registry, not a colour registry: qualification is documented descent from the foundation sires Max and Patches, so a Rangerbred need not be spotted. That is what the two strains say - eleven founders in twenty are solid, nine carry the leopard complex.

The solid strain forces the leopard complex and both PATN modifiers wild outright rather than leaving them unnamed, because that is the breed's actual claim about itself and is worth reading in the file.
Leopard is deliberately lighter here than in the Appaloosa and the Knabstrupper: the Rangerbred is a leopard breed, not the defining one.

Pinto is barred by the registry within five generations, so there is no tobiano, frame, splash or W-series dominant white in either strain. Sabino 1 is kept light, for ordinary face and leg white only.

All disorders clear. The draft offered PSSM1 at 1.5% as an admitted guess for the Quarter Horse outcrosses; no Rangerbred-specific rate exists, and GYS1 is dominant, so every copy would show. Approved-outcross ancestry is not a licence to import Quarter Horse rates.
Congenital stationary night blindness on LP/LP is already modelled by the leopard locus. Equine recurrent uveitis is a multifactorial risk, not a single locus, and is folded into heartiness.
Documented descent, registry inspection, the dished Arabian profile, cattle sense and endurance conditioning are all outside what the mod models.

name: Connemara Pony
notes: Sturdy compact good bone, often grey. OCD / laminitis are age-related (folded into heartiness).

name: Criollo
notes: The Argentine or Rio de la Plata Criollo, not every horse called Criollo across the Americas - the regional populations differ in size, gait and use, and one shared pool would erase that. The gaucho's cattle and distance horse, into the Argentine Rural Society studbook in 1918 and restored to type by Solanet afterwards.

Dun is the breed: seven founders in ten are the traditional strain, where dun dominates and a double copy is ordinary, giving bay dun, red dun and grullo with a dorsal stripe and leg barring. The other three in ten are the broader palette, with dun a minority and more cream.
The two strains differ only in dun and cream. A strain may override gene pools and nothing else, so they cannot differ in size, and the size band spans both.

Tobiano is forced wild: the shared southern-Criollo standard excludes paint and tobiano, and the broad summaries that say 'pinto' use the word loosely. Frame overo and a little splash are allowed instead, which is the overo the sources actually describe - and O/O is the lethal white cross, the one breeding hazard here.

Manchado is named, at carriers only. This mod has the locus and the Criollo is the population it is most reported in; the pattern is a suspected rare recessive with no test and no measured frequency, so the 6% carrier rate is a design call, not data. It makes the Criollo the one breed where two carriers can throw a manchado foal.
No leopard complex: nothing found establishes appaloosa spotting as a Criollo founder trait.
All disorders clear, PSSM1 included. It is dominant, so a guessed rate would show on every copy, and no Criollo-specific survey exists.

Health 10 is the point of the breed - endurance, thrift, sound feet and coping with sparse forage. Real endurance trials, grazing efficiency, cow sense, hoof density and the full mane and tail are not modelled.

name: Croatian Coldblood
notes: The Hrvatski hladnokrvnjak, Croatia's principal heavy farm and forestry horse - lowland Slavonia, Podravina, Posavina, Medimurje and the Sava and Drava basins, local mares over Brabant, Noriker, Ardennes and Percheron.
The taller, heavier counterpart to the Posavac. The two are distinct but genetically related populations, and here the difference is the size band and a lower speed and jump, not the coat.

Chestnut-led on purpose: chestnut is the visual core, with bay and brown behind it and black a minority. The draft's own E/e split put chestnut at under a fifth, which contradicted its prose, so extension was tilted until chestnut actually leads. No Croatian studbook coat survey exists - these are gameplay approximations and nothing more.
Grey, dun, roan and flaxen chestnut are real minorities. Cream, pearl, champagne, silver and mushroom are forced wild: nothing found supports them in a conservative founder pool.
Solid-bodied. No tobiano, frame, splash, dominant white or leopard - this is a traditional farm horse, not a colour-bred pinto. Sabino 1 and rabicano sit near absent, for ordinary markings only.
No wild herds: a managed agricultural breed, so the cowboy, the stables and the egg are the only ways to one.
Heat sensitive, lightly - a broad heavy draught sheds heat poorly, as with the Belgian and the Clydesdale - and cold tolerant for continental winters in wet lowland and forest.
All disorders clear. PSSM1 is the tempting mistake: it is dominant, it varies sharply by bloodline, and 'draught breed' is not evidence of a Croatian Coldblood rate.
Traction, harness work, ploughing, logging, fertility, moderate fetlock feathering, broad hooves and floodplain footing are none of them modelled.

name: Dales Pony
notes: Heavy feathering, dense bone, hardy moorland type - feathering is a roadmap render item.
EMS / laminitis: age-related, folded into heartiness.

name: Danubian
notes: The Dunavski kon, one of Bulgaria's modern national breeds - built at the Klementina stud near Pleven out of local mares and imported Nonius stock, for the army and to improve the local working horse, and recognised in 1951.
A light draught and carriage horse: the middle ground between the Hungarian Nonius and a sport horse. Strong and harness-minded without being a heavy draught or a trotter.

Dark and solid, and only just varied. Extension, agouti and a trace of flaxen are the whole colour pool; grey, cream, pearl, champagne, silver, mushroom, dun and roan are all forced wild, because no Danubian source supports seeding them. The base-colour weights are gameplay approximations - the breed's own genetic survey is microsatellite diversity and sire lines, not coat loci.
No pinto and no leopard. Sabino 1 and rabicano sit at 2%, for ordinary markings only.

The six paternal lines - Zdravko, Nonius XVII-30, Torpedo, Lider, Kalifa and Hrabar - are genealogical, not coat strains, so they are deliberately not modelled as strains. The survey behind them found high diversity and low inbreeding, which is why the pool is varied rather than fixed on one dark colour.
No wild herds: a managed Bulgarian working breed, so the cowboy, the stables and the egg only.
All disorders clear. A Nonius foundation is not a licence to copy Nonius assumptions, and a working breed is not a licence to copy draught PSSM1 estimates.
Harness action, pulling force, remount suitability, hoof durability and leg bone are not modelled.

name: Dartmoor Pony
notes: Small, large head, thick mane and tail. Laminitis / EMS are age-related (folded into heartiness).

name: Debao Pony
notes: The Debao ai ma, or Baiseshishan pony - a registered landrace of Debao county in western Guangxi, descended from the older Guoxia tradition but a distinct breed from it, not another name for it. One of the smallest horses in the world.

Rediscovered by a 1981 field survey that turned up a seven-year-old mare only 92.5 cm at the withers; research from 1986 to 1990 established that the small stature is stable and heritable and separated the breed from the taller Baise horse.

The coat pool is built to a real survey - 856 ponies, reported as 54.9% bay, 15.8% grey, 15.0% chestnut, 6.8% black, 3.3% rabbit-brown, 2.5% yellow and 1.9% piebald - which makes it one of the few breeds here whose colour rates are measured rather than designed.
The survey's 'yellow' and 'piebald' are read as cream and tobiano. The source does not identify either molecularly, so those two are visual proxies and the weakest part of the pool.
The survey's 'rabbit-brown' is read as pangare, which the intake draft left unmapped. A mealy light-brown is the best available reading of the category, and it is a guess.

Genomic work puts the miniature size down to selection near TBX3 and HMGA2, arrived at independently of the small stature of other pony breeds. Neither is named as a pool here: the mod's HMGA2 is the p.G28E pony test and this is not that result, so the size band carries it instead - the same call the Domestic Mountain Pony made.
Its smallness is a normal breed phenotype, not dwarfism. ACAN is clear on purpose and borrowing a dwarfism allele would be a different, sicker animal.
Dun, pearl, champagne, silver, mushroom, flaxen, roan, rabicano and leopard are all forced wild. Sabino 1 sits low, for the limited face and lower-leg white the survey mentions.
Heat tolerant for subtropical Guangxi; no cold locus.
All disorders clear. No Debao-specific carrier rate was found for any of them.
Steep limestone country, hard hoof horn, dense mane and fetlock hair, pack carriage far beyond what the size suggests, and the modern pony-polo and youth-riding roles are none of them modelled.

name: Dhampir
description: A night horse with blood-red eyes and glowing whites. Most are seal brown and only a little stronger than an ordinary horse; one in ten is white from nose to tail, three times as hard to kill, burned by daylight, and able to heal only by biting something living.
notes: Two strains, never a mix: white with two copies of magic white, sun sensitivity, blood diet and the vampiric stat allele; or seal brown carrying one silent copy of each.
Every founder has red irises with glowing scleras.
Two seal browns throw a magic white foal one time in four, but the whole animal - white, sun-sensitive, blood-drinking and doubled on all three stats - only one time in 4096.

name: Dolahest
notes: The Dolahest or Dole Gudbrandsdal - Norway's largest native horse, from Gudbrandsdalen and the eastern valleys. A cold-blood that did everything a Norwegian farm needed: timber, fields, carts, sleighs, roads and riding.
The spelling here drops the slash from Dolahest because a breed id is a lower-case ASCII token.

More colourful than the silhouette suggests, and the point of difference from the Fjord: the current Norwegian breeding plan accepts black, brown, chestnut, buckskin, palomino and every grey, where the Fjord is effectively colour-fixed. Cream is real here.

Dun is forced wild on conflicting evidence. Some secondary summaries list it, other sources say the dun allele does not occur in the breed, and no Dole survey was found either way - so the conservative reading shipped.

Silver, pearl, champagne, mushroom and flaxen are forced wild, and so is every white pattern: moderate facial markings and low socks are allowed by the plan but extensive white is restricted at inspection, and the mod's white-pattern loci all paint far more than that. Sabino 1 sits near absent for ordinary markings only.

The lighter Dole Trotter (Doletrav) is a real sub-tradition and is not a strain here: no separate height was cited for it, and a strain may override gene pools and nothing else, so it could not have its own size band anyway.
Cold tolerant near-fixed - bred to pull through snow - and lightly heat sensitive as the heavy cold-bloods are.
Two height figures were cited and the current breed plan's 148-156 cm was followed over NordGen's 145-155 cm.
All disorders clear. The breed's endangered status is not evidence of disease prevalence and was not turned into any.
The national Dole organisation formed in 1947 and the breed is managed today through the Norwegian Horse Centre as one of Norway's endangered natives.
Timber traction, harness trotting and the limited feathering are none of them modelled.

name: Domestic Mountain Pony
notes: The Domaci brdski konj, or Bosnian Mountain Horse - the only indigenous domestic horse of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a Dinaric pack, riding and farm pony. Selective breeding began at Gorazde in 1908 and concentrated at the Borike and Han Pijesak studs, with Arab stallions used at Borike to improve it.
Also the Bosanski brdski konj, which is the form its own breeders' association uses.

This is the rare breed here with real coat data: Cotman et al. genotyped 313 horses from the association's records and found dark bay 44%, black 36%, ordinary bay 11% and dun 8%, with the true-dun D allele at 0.09. The pool is built to that rather than to a generic mountain-pony guess, and it is the only breed in the mod whose dun rate is a published allele frequency instead of a design call.

Its small size is selected, not carried: a genome-wide homozygosity scan (Schrimpf et al.) found long-term selection toward roughly 135 cm at the withers and a high prevalence of small-allele homozygosity at the body-size loci examined. That is not the p.G28E pony test, so no HMGA2 pool is named here - the size band carries it instead.

Dark bay is carried by the shade locus, not by a separate agouti allele. At as a real allele was dropped (owner's call), and seal sits at the top of agouti's shade band, so the shade pool is skewed dark instead of using the house-standard spread - a/a gives the 36% black, and the A_ horses come out mostly dark rather than ordinary bay.
Chestnut is functionally absent: the breeding programme excludes it, and e sits at 0.01 only as an admission of modelling uncertainty rather than as a colour anyone will see.

One honest discrepancy: D at 0.09 makes about 17% of founders dun, where the same study classified only 8% as dun by eye. The study itself reports phenotype-genotype mismatches at this locus, so the measured allele frequency was followed rather than the visual tally.
d1 is carried on purpose - primitive marking without body dilution, which is how a population whose visual dun classification proved unreliable should look.

Grey, cream, pearl, champagne, silver, mushroom and flaxen are all forced wild, and so is every white pattern: the programme allows all colours except grey, pinto, chestnut and spotted, and requires no white markings. No roan, no rabicano, no leopard, no sabino.
Cold tolerant for Dinaric winters and lightly heat tolerant for the dry summers. Health 10 is the hardiness, fertility and low-input survival the breed is known for.
All disorders clear. Arab improvement crosses do not license Arabian SCID, CA or LFS rates, and a sturdy mountain build does not license a draught PSSM1 rate.

Hoof hardness, mountain traction, carrying capacity, the Agan, Barut and Misko stallion lines, and the split between the lighter riding and heavier pack types are not modelled. A strain may override gene pools and nothing else, so the two types cannot differ in size here; the band spans both.

name: Exmoor Pony
notes: Mealy muzzle and eye rings - the breed standard, and near-fixed here. Double-layered winter coat - cosmetic, out of scope.
An ancient, exceptionally hardy landrace - no white, no dilutions.

name: Falabella
notes: The smallest breed - the size band sits against the MAGICAL_MIN_SCALE guard.
'Fragile bones' left as very low heartiness rather than a lethal gene.

name: Fell Pony
notes: The pony of the northern fells - Cumbria and the Lake District. Packed lead down from the northern mines and moved farm goods over ground too wet, rocky, steep and narrow for a horse.

Black first, dark brown second, then bay and a little grey: the registered palette is black, brown, bay and grey, and black only became predominant in the second half of the twentieth century - bay and brown were especially common before that. The agouti pool is weighted to that phenotype rather than being a published allele frequency.
Chestnut, piebald and skewbald go in Section X rather than the main colour standard, so chestnut sits at about one founder in two hundred and no pinto locus is named at all.
Dark brown is carried by the shade locus, so the shade pool is skewed dark rather than using the house-standard spread.

Cream, pearl, silver, dun, champagne, mushroom, flaxen, roan, rabicano and leopard are all forced wild - none is a standard mainstream Fell colour. Sabino 1 sits at 1% for the permitted star and the odd white hind hoof; extensive facial white and white forelegs are discouraged by the standard.

Foal Immunodeficiency Syndrome is the breed's defining modern health story and this file cannot carry it: FIS is a fatal autosomal-recessive that the mod has no locus for. A foundational screen found 82 carriers in 214 Fell Ponies - about 38%, and UC Davis has reported near 40% - and the same mutation is present in the Dales Pony. Testing has been available since 2010. The gene is on the roadmap; its absence here is a missing feature, not a claim that the breed is clear.
Every other disorder is clear - no credible Fell-specific evidence was found for any of them.
Cold tolerant partially, as the neighbouring Dales is: a weatherproof hill pony with a dense winter coat.
The Fell Pony Society registry formed in 1922; the RBST puts the type in the Lake District for more than two thousand years.
Blue horn, the silky feather to the knee, the dense winter coat and the economical all-day walk are none of them modelled.

name: Finnhorse
notes: The Suomenhevonen - Finland's only native horse, and its national one. A northern farm-and-harness horse rather than a continental warmblood: forestry, fields, sleighs, cavalry, and now harness trotting.

Chestnut with a flaxen mane and tail is the breed, and it is a policy outcome rather than an ancient trait. The studbook closed in 1907 and twentieth-century policy refused colours it called foreign - grey, palomino, piebald, white - driving chestnut past 90% of the modern population. Flaxen is near-fixed on top of it.

The old diversity was not wholly erased, and this is the rare pool where the heritage minorities are the interesting part: bay at about 6% and black at about 1.2% (2007 figures), plus surviving traces of grey, cream, silver, dun, roan, rabicano and splash white 1, each at a percent or two.
Tobiano sits at four founders in a thousand. A single historical pinto is on record and piebalds were actively selected against; this preserves the outlier without creating a pinto population.

Sabino 1 is deliberately absent even though the breed has a moderately common minimally-expressed sabino-like pattern. That pattern is documented as non-SB1, so naming the mod's SB1 would assert a molecular result nobody has shown.

The four official sections since 1971 - trotter, riding, pony-sized, working - are NOT strains here. They are performance and inspection categories over one shared gene pool, earned individually and not inherited, so encoding them would invent four closed sub-breeds that do not exist. The size band spans them; only the pony section has a hard limit (148 cm) and only the general average (155-156 cm) is otherwise pinned.
Cold tolerant near-fixed, for Finnish winters, bogs and forest.
Flaxen's architecture is still incompletely resolved in the literature, so the near-fixed rate here is a gameplay reading of a visual hallmark, not a molecular frequency.

All disorders clear. The breed has real population-genetic concerns - one analysis put nuclear effective population near 50 per section against high mitochondrial variation - but a bottleneck is not a disease rate.
Uncommon rather than rare: the draft asked for rare, but this is a living national breed in regular harness use, not a remnant.
The trotting gait, the modest feathering and the thick mane and tail are none of them modelled.

name: Norwegian Fjord
notes: The two-tone mane (dark midtstol, pale guard hair) and the primitive stripes both come from the near-fixed dun; the erect clip that shows them off is grooming, and is not modelled.
Almost every Fjord is a dun (brown/red/grey/white/yellow dun); E_ a/a + D drives the classic brown dun.
EMS: age-related, folded into heartiness.

name: Florida Cracker Horse
notes: Florida's state horse since 2008, and a colonial-Spanish descendant of horses landed by Spanish expeditions in the early 1500s. The name comes from the Florida cowhunters nicknamed for the crack of their rawhide whips; the horses inherited it.

A cattle horse for palmetto scrub, pine flatwoods, wet prairie and swamp margin - all day, on little feed, picking its own footing. Health 10 is that, not bulk: it is a small light riding horse of 700 to 1,000 pounds, not a Quarter Horse.

A broad palette for a heritage stock breed - bay, dark bay, black, brown, grey, chestnut, dun and grullo, with roan and pinto strains persisting - but it still skews dark and practical, so the shade pool is skewed dark and dun is a visible recurring quarter of the herd rather than a signature.
Grullo is dun over black, and dun carries the dorsal stripe, leg bars and shoulder cross the breed is known for. A little d1 rides along: primitive marking without body dilution.

Cream, pearl, champagne, silver and mushroom are forced wild - not documented as central colours, though they can enter by outcrossing. Frame overo is forced wild too, which deliberately keeps lethal white out of a small conservation breed with no evidence for it.
Leopard is forced wild: Appaloosa-type spotting is not part of the documented core palette.

DMRT3 gait is not named. The breed is famous for a smooth ground-covering way of going, but no source put that in the gait-keeper sense, and the Boerperd and the Paso breeds are where this file would have had to borrow from.
Heat tolerant partially, as the Banker Horse is. Tolerating heat and insects on open range was a working requirement, not a comfort.

All disorders clear, and deliberately so: the breed was displaced from Florida cattle work by the Quarter Horse in the 1930s, which is a shared history and not a licence to import the Quarter Horse disorder panel.
The registry formed in 1989 after the 1930s collapse. Older accounts insist you cannot judge one by looking - the best way to recognise one is to ride it.
Cow sense, quick acceleration, the white sclera, hard feet and insect tolerance are none of them modelled.

name: Friesian
notes: Jet black, heavy feathering, thick wavy mane and tail. Fixed E/E a/a, no white or dilution genes at all.
Feathering + wavy mane: roadmap render items.
Dwarfism, megaesophagus: dwarfism exists (ACAN); megaesophagus carried at the wild rate too.

name: Gelderlander
notes: The Gelders Paard of eastern Gelderland, once the Basispaard - the big chestnut carriage warmblood with white socks and an elevated trot. Solid and old-fashioned next to a modern sport horse, and never draught-heavy.
Chestnut is the traditional and most frequent colour, which is why extension is tilted red - about a third of founders. Bay and black are real variety behind it and grey is uncommon.

The white is the point: broad blazes and substantial socks are part of the look, so sabino 1 is heavy at about a third of founders with the W20 booster and a light splash behind it. This is the markings mechanism, not a pinto pool.
Tobiano sits at a twentieth - skewbald is rare but historically present, a memorable find rather than the default.

Cream, pearl, champagne, silver, mushroom, dun, roan and leopard are forced wild - none is central to the reviewed standard. Frame overo is forced wild too, with no evidence for it and lethal white as the cost of guessing.

Warmblood Fragile Foal Syndrome is the real modern genetic concern in the Dutch warmblood population - the KWPN requires licensed stallions to be tested so carriers are not paired - and the mod has no WFFS locus, so no rate is written. It is on the roadmap. PLOD1 is NOT a substitute: the mod's PLOD1 is Friesian dwarfism and they are different disorders that happen to share a gene name in loose writing.
Every other disorder is clear; no Gelderlander-specific carrier study was found.
No heat or cold locus - a Dutch lowland carriage horse has no climate history to carry, so it is neutral everywhere.

The Geldersch Paarden Stamboek was founded in 1890 around two goals, an agricultural carriage horse and a luxury one. In 1965 it was one of the two foundation breeds of the Dutch Warmblood with the heavier Groninger, and was later folded under the KWPN; a Classic Gelder studbook won Dutch recognition in 2019 specifically to stop the historical type being absorbed.
Scarce: a 2017 estimate put it at about 600 breeding mares and 35 stallions.
The high-stepping carriage trot, the upright neck set and the broad durable hoof are none of them modelled.

name: Gotland Pony
notes: The Gotlandsruss, or just the Russ - the island landrace of Gotland in the Baltic. Older names are better: Skogruss, the little horse of the woods, and Skogsbaggar, forest rams.

Dun is the signature family and sits near three-quarters of founders, over a bay-led base, so bay dun leads with grullo and red dun behind it. d1 is carried on purpose - primitive marking without body dilution, which is what a landrace should look like.

Single cream is deliberately present and double cream deliberately impossible: the Swedish conservation description excludes homozygous cream, not cream itself, so Cr/N ships and Cr/Cr does not. A founder will never be cremello, though breeding two carriers still can be.
Grey and tobiano are excluded by the same conservation profile and are forced wild outright, not merely kept rare.

No gait locus, and for once that is measured rather than assumed: a published sample of 28 Gotland ponies found the DMRT3 gait-keeper allele at zero frequency. The breed's sporting reputation is pony trotting, which is a trot.

Champagne, silver, mushroom, pearl, roan, rabicano, leopard and every white-pattern locus are forced wild - no breed-specific evidence for any. Flaxen is the one cautious aesthetic addition and is not a documented population estimate.
Cold tolerant partially: wind-exposed Baltic country - mixed forest, heath, thin soils and cold wet winters rather than lush pasture - and a managed semi-feral herd still lives out at Lojsta Hed.

It came within a hair of ending. By 1922 the core remnant was seven mares, one young stallion and six young horses; Welsh and Welsh Mountain stallions were brought in in 1951 and 1957 against the inbreeding and their lines run through the modern population, with no outside introductions since.
Uncommon rather than rare on the numbers: NordGen recorded about 2,500 mares in Sweden in 2020 and conservation sources put the world population at roughly 6,000 to 8,000.
All disorders clear. Importing Arabian, Quarter Horse, Friesian or warmblood rates into a small Swedish pony population would be inventing them.
The famously hard sound hooves, the pony-trotting talent and the long back are none of them modelled.

name: Guoxia
notes: The 'under-fruit-tree horse' of Debao, Jingxi and Tianyang in the Baise region of western Guangxi, and the name is literal: a pony small enough to walk beneath orchard branches. One of the smallest horses in the world, at roughly 86 to 100 cm with an average near 97.

A functional mountain pony and not a purpose-bred miniature pet - narrow paths, small farms, pack work, light draught and local riding in rugged subtropical hill country. Unusually generous hair for a southern pony: abundant mane and tail, and thick leg hair.

Three traditional colours - bay, grey and roan - so bay leads with grey a recognisable but not dominant minority and roan below it. No breed-specific coat study was located; these are conservative gameplay estimates.

Dun is forced wild ON PURPOSE, and this is the interesting call in the file. Sources describe primitive markings, but nobody has shown those markings are the tested TBX3 dun allele, and claiming otherwise would assert a molecular result that does not exist. The markings belong in flavour and model art until someone genotypes one.

ACAN is clear and no dwarfism allele is borrowed. The smallness is a normal breed phenotype selected for over a long time, not a pathology, and the size band carries it - the same call the Debao Pony and the Domestic Mountain Pony made.
Every dilution and every white pattern beyond roan is forced wild, with no breed-specific evidence for any of them.
Heat tolerant partially, for southern China's subtropical hill country.

Often called ancient and often said to carry Mongolian-horse ancestry, though no continuous studbook supports either. Its modern identity really dates from rediscovery: a remote herd of roughly a thousand very small ponies was reported in 1981, after which a registry was founded and 390 animals registered.
All disorders clear. Do not import disease rates from superficially similar small breeds.
Shares its home region with the Baise Horse and the Debao Pony, which are separate breeds from it and from each other.
The notably strong feet, the abundant hair and the orchard-height niche are none of them modelled.

name: Gypsy Vanner
notes: 'Drum' cobby body, heavy feathering, abundant mane and tail - feathering + mane are roadmap render items. Usually tobiano pinto.
CPL, EMS: age-related, folded into heartiness.

name: Hackney
notes: Upright neck, high knee action - gait/animation is a roadmap item (DMRT3). Refined bone.
Osteoarthritis: age-related, folded into heartiness.

name: Haflinger
notes: Chestnut body with a striking flaxen mane and tail, and the breed the flaxen locus is calibrated against. Fixed e/e keeps it chestnut.
EMS / laminitis: age-related, folded into heartiness.

name: Hanoverian
notes: Powerful large-framed uphill warmblood, bred for jumping and dressage.
OCD, navicular: age-related, folded into heartiness.

name: Henson Horse
notes: The Cheval Henson of the Bay of Somme and the Marquenterre in Picardy - the horse of the bay, and one of the youngest breeds in this book. Made in the 1970s from Norwegian Fjord stallions over local French saddle mares, and officially recognised as a French breed in July 2003.

The design brief was explicit: keep the Fjord's calm, its primitive dun colour, its strength and its ability to live outdoors, and make it taller, longer-legged and more comfortable for trekking. It reads as a refined, less heavy Fjord.

Bay dun - baie sauvage - every time, and this is the most tightly fixed colour pool here after the Friesian and the Camargue. Extension is fixed E so no founder is ever a red dun, agouti is fixed A so none is ever a grullo, and every founder carries D.
The dorsal stripe is compulsory in the standard and leg bars are common, which is what the dun does here. d1 and d2 ride along behind D without ever showing, since one D is enough.
Grey, cream, pearl, champagne, silver, mushroom and flaxen are forced wild, and so is every white pattern - extensive white is discouraged in the breed and prohibited outright in breeding stallions.

Pangare is not named, which is the one place this file may be wrong. The Fjord's near-fixed pangare is part of the look it was bred from, but the intake draft never raised it and inventing a rate for a fifty-year-old breed on the strength of its foundation sire is a guess too far. Worth revisiting if the Henson looks too flat beside a Fjord.
The real breeding rule of roughly 25 to 50 percent Fjord ancestry is not modelled; nor is the two-toned black-and-gold mane, which is the other half of the Fjord inheritance.
Cold tolerant partially, for a coastal Picardy climate lived outdoors year-round on sand, wet grassland and estuary marsh.
All disorders clear. No Henson-specific carrier data was located, which for a breed this young and this closely managed is unsurprising.

Rare, and genuinely small: a historical count put about 1,200 in France with some 200 around the Marquenterre, and few active stallions means inbreeding avoidance is a live concern. That figure is historical and not a current census.
It is named for the bay, not for a person or a stud, and it turned a regional tourism idea into a recognised breed.
The preferred dark hooves, the beach and estuary footing, and its suitability for novice riders are none of them modelled.

name: Hequ
notes: The horse of the great bend of the Yellow River, on the Qinghai-Tibetan plateau where Qinghai, southern Gansu and western Sichuan meet. Formerly called the Nanfan.

Its home ground is around eleven thousand feet. Health 10 is the mod's only available proxy for that: thin air, cold winters, seasonal forage, carrying a rider all day and recovering afterwards where a lowland horse would not. Oxygen physiology, acclimatisation and haemoglobin response are not modelled and cannot be.

Three regional varieties ship as strains, and grey is the whole of the difference. Jiaode of southern Gansu is the largest and heaviest and much the greyest; Suoke of western Sichuan is compact with a high tail carriage; Kesheng of Qinghai is the balanced all-rounder and carries historical Mongolian influence.
The varieties really do differ in size as well as colour, and cannot here: a strain may override gene pools and nothing else, so the one size band spans all three.

Black, bay and brown, and grey - true progressive grey, born dark and lightening with age, not silver dapple and not mouse dun. Every dilution, every white pattern and the leopard complex are forced wild.
No representative genotype study exists for extension, agouti or grey by variety. These are calibrated gameplay approximations and not Chinese studbook percentages.
Cold tolerant near-fixed, for plateau winters; no heat locus.

All disorders clear, with the reasoning spelled out because it is the tempting kind of breed to guess on: PSSM1 is dominant and not a carrier allele at all, the Arabian panel of SCID, CA and LFS is not licensed by any oriental influence, the Quarter Horse panel of HYPP, GBED and HERDA has nothing to do with a plateau landrace, and warmblood WFFS is not a default mountain-horse mutation.

Some sources trace the regional identity to Tang-era horse culture, and Suoke's high tail carriage does resemble Tang art. It is a long-developed highland landrace all the same, not a relic of one dynasty.
The broad hooves, the large mobile eyes and long open ears, and the light draught and local racing roles are none of them modelled.

name: Highland Pony
notes: One of the largest British native ponies, and one of Scotland's three native breeds with the Shetland and the Eriskay. Carried deer off the hills, hauled timber, ploughed crofts and packed over roadless ground, and some still carry deer down from Scottish hills today.

Dun is the signature and the breed has a whole vocabulary for it - mouse, yellow, grey, cream, red or fox, oatmeal, biscuit - with dorsal stripes, leg barring and the occasional shoulder stripe. Roughly four founders in five carry D.
Two different greys are in play and they are independent here: 'grey dun' is a dun shade, and the grey gene is the separate thing that whitens a horse with age. Both are in the pool and they combine.
Cream carries the cream dun and biscuit dun end of that vocabulary. It is an approximation - the sources describe phenotype categories, not MATP allele counts.
Flaxen carries the occasional liver chestnut with a light silvery mane and tail that the registry also accepts.

Every white-pattern locus is forced wild, and unusually this is the registry's own rule rather than an absence of evidence: broken colours are not permitted, a small star is acceptable, and white legs, extensive facial white, white hooves and - on stallions - anything beyond that small star are unacceptable. So no sabino pool at all, not even a token one.
Champagne, silver, mushroom and pearl are forced wild with no defensible breed-specific basis.
Cold tolerant near-fixed: heather, bog, loose stone, thin grazing and a wet climate, with a dense double winter coat that sheds to a clean summer one.

Health 10 is the easy-keeper constitution - real strength in sparse country. The modern flip side is obesity, laminitis and metabolic trouble on rich pasture, which is a management phenotype and not a single-locus disease, so nothing is coded for it.
All disorders clear; no trustworthy Highland-specific carrier study was found, and importing rates from breeds where those diseases are established would be inventing them.

The registry began in the 1830s and the Highland Pony Society was formally established in 1923. Queen Victoria favoured the breed and Queen Elizabeth II kept a substantial working Highland stud at Balmoral. The Society manages co-ancestry with the SPARKS kinship system, which warns against pairings expected to yield 10% or more co-ancestry.
The silky feathering, the tough round feet, the double coat and the food-motivated stubbornness are none of them modelled.

name: Hucul Pony
notes: The Carpathian pony of the Hutsul region - Hutsul, Huzul, Hucul, all the same horse. A low, deep, short-legged mountain worker with hooves sound enough that many are never shod.

Filed under Romania on the owner's breed-by-country table. The homeland genuinely spans the Eastern Carpathians across Romania, Ukraine, Poland and Slovakia, with breeding populations in Hungary, the Czech Republic and Austria, and Poland holds the international Studbook of Origin - but a breed is pinned to one nation here, not a region.

The colour pool follows the published Polish allele-frequency study rather than the second draft's gameplay estimates, which is why agouti is split near the middle and black is a real quarter of the herd rather than a rarity.

That same choice makes dun a visible minority of about a quarter rather than the signature it reads as in prose. The measured d frequency was 0.878. This is the Domestic Mountain Pony situation again - a measured allele frequency disagreeing with the visual reputation - and the measurement won. A 2019 study found recorded Hucul colours disagreeing with genotype often enough to justify the choice.

d1 is carried on purpose: primitive marking without body dilution, which is much of what the dorsal stripe and zebra leg barring look like in a population whose dun classification is unreliable by eye.
Grey is forced wild. The measured study found it essentially absent at 0.003 and the international standard excludes it outright, so the two lines of evidence agree for once.

Tobiano is the one place the two drafts could not be reconciled and the value here splits them. The study measured To at 0.071, which would make one founder in eight a pinto; the studbook admits skewbald only as a rare historical colour, attributed to old oriental blood. Seven percent of founders carrying it is the compromise and it is a judgement call, not a measurement.
Cream, pearl, champagne, silver, mushroom, flaxen, roan, rabicano, leopard and every other white-pattern locus are forced wild - no defensible Hucul-specific evidence for any.
Cold tolerant near-fixed: Carpathian slopes, high pasture and stony ground, lived on grass and hay rather than in a stable for much of the year.
All disorders clear. The conservation literature on this breed is about inbreeding and bottleneck management, not single-locus disease frequency.

First mentioned in professional accounts as early as 1613, with systematic recording from the imperial stud at Luczyn in Bukovina in 1856. The studbook is closed and requires five documented generations on both sides, with DNA verification since 2002. The FAO listed it in its protected gene fund for primitive breeds in 1979 and the Hucul International Federation has coordinated the national populations since 1994; peer-reviewed work has called it a vanishing breed, which is why it ships rare and not uncommon.
The Hucul Path trail-and-obstacle competition, the hard unshod hooves and the thick mane and tail are none of them modelled.

name: Icelandic Horse
notes: Thick double coat, short legs, long back - the tölt (extra gait) is a roadmap item (DMRT3). Extremely varied colours; extremely hardy.

name: Irish Draught
notes: Scopey powerful frame, strong clean limbs - the classic sport-horse foundation. Joint stress is age-related (folded into heartiness).

The Horse Sport Ireland standard asks for any strong whole colour and names six - bay, brown, grey, chestnut, black and dun - and calls excessive white undesirable. That named list is why dun is in the pool at all, and why no white pattern is.

Two pools sit outside that list and are kept as shipped rather than re-tuned: roan, and a trace of cream. Neither is among the six named colours, so they are the open question on this breed's palette.

PSSM1 (GYS1) has been detected in the breed, but no Irish Draught population frequency is published and the mutation is dominant, so it ships clear rather than at a guessed rate that would show on every copy.

158-170 cm, and a horse built to work and still move freely - not a draught horse in the continental sense. Inspection scores, Irish Draught percentage and Irish Sport Horse eligibility are not modelled.

name: Jutland
notes: The Jydsk hest - Denmark's national draught horse, out of the local workhorses of the Jutland peninsula and organised into a studbook late in the nineteenth century. Suffolk Punch blood is in it, which is visible here in the pool as well as in the silhouette.

Flaxen chestnut is the whole player-facing identity: a red body with a cream-to-blond mane, tail and feather. Chestnut is near-led rather than fixed, because the deliberate twentieth-century selection that produced the modern 'national colour' did not erase the older bay and black horses.
The pale mane is flaxen and not cream. Cream is forced wild on purpose - a palomino Jutland would be the wrong horse, and the draft's own rationale says so.

Grey, roan and silver are historically recorded and are kept at a couple of percent each. Silver is the weakest of the three: it rests on secondary breed descriptions with no Jutland PMEL17 count behind it, and on a chestnut-led breed it is invisible most of the time it is carried.
A medium draught, not a giant. The size band is the cited 157-164 cm and lands below the Shire and the Percheron on purpose; the breed's mass is in its width, which is not modelled.

Managed sources only. The population fell under 300 horses in 1998 and Danish conservation work brought it back near 2,000 by 2016, which is a recovering national breed rather than anything a player should find running loose.
All disorders clear. No Jutland-specific carrier rate was located for any locus, and a heavy draught build is not on its own a licence to seed PSSM1.
Moderately cold tolerant for Danish winters - a northern farm horse, but a lowland maritime one, so not the near-fixed pool the Nordic mountain breeds carry.
The heavy mane and tail, the feathering, real pulling force, harness work and the conservation registry itself are none of them modelled.

name: Kaimanawa
notes: The feral horses of the Kaimanawa Ranges in the central North Island of Aotearoa New Zealand. Not a closed breed: the Department of Conservation describes them as mixed-breed ferals with a strong Thoroughbred and station-hack likeness, mustered periodically to hold the herd near 300 head.

The base pool follows the field tally - roughly 56% bay, 26% chestnut and 7.7% black - rather than the draft's own allele figures, which would have produced chestnut at a twentieth of the observed rate.

The two strains are the real geographic split and the only one the mod can carry. Every sampled grey horse belonged to one maternal haplogroup and every one of them was in the south; the chestnuts concentrate in the north. So the Northern strain forces grey wild entirely and the Southern strain is near-fixed for it over a darker base, which is what makes its foals come out bay or black and whiten later.
Grey in the base pool is the population-wide rate, and only reaches a founder that the strain roll leaves it to.
Every white-pattern locus is forced wild. Face and lower-leg white is common in field descriptions of these horses, and ordinary markings are not evidence of a pinto allele.
All disorders clear. No Kaimanawa-specific carrier frequency exists, and a feral population's ancestry is not a reason to import the disease panel of the breeds behind it.
Health 10 is unmanaged survival on volcanic tussock country: no feed, no shelter, no farrier, and a population that persists anyway.
Lightly cold tolerant for the Central Plateau's winters rather than near-fixed - high country, but not a Nordic one.

Only six maternal and six paternal lineages were found in 96 sampled horses, and mitochondrial diversity is lower than in several other feral populations. A bottleneck is not a disease rate and was not turned into one.
The muster, the herd structure and the adoption programme are not modelled.

name: Karabair
notes: The Qorabayir - an old Central Asian riding and light-harness horse of the oasis country, kept above all in Uzbekistan and across the border into northern Tajikistan. Uzbek writing calls it a golden fund of the national horse breeding, and it is used for riding, packing, light draught and the mounted games.

The name is usually glossed 'black horse' and the breed is not colour-defined. Bay, chestnut, grey and black are all documented, with no registry colour rule; recent Uzbek literature leans on black and dark bay, which the extension and agouti pools carry rather than an artificial dark shade band.
Grey is a real and visible part of the population at something near a fifth of founders. The rate is a gameplay estimate, not a measured STX17 frequency - no such count exists for the breed.
Every dilution and every white pattern is forced wild. That is an absence of breed-specific evidence rather than a registry prohibition, and it is the conservative reading.
The real main, riding and denser intra-breed types are not strains here. No separate size or colour data was cited for them, and a strain may override gene pools and nothing else.
Tolerant both ways for a continental climate - hot dry summers, cold winters - and neither near-fixed, since this is oasis and foothill stock rather than a high-desert or high-plateau landrace.
All disorders clear. The one breed-health source found states outright that no inherited disease is well documented in the Karabair, while cautioning that absence of evidence is not proof of absence.
The traditional gaits, the mounted games and the regional type differences are none of them modelled.

name: Karabakh
notes: Small head, muscular arched neck, golden sheen - the sheen is not modelled (a shader).

name: Karakachan Horse
notes: The horse of the Karakachans, the transhumant pastoralists of the Balkans, and an indigenous Bulgarian mountain breed of the Rhodopes, Rila, Pirin, Stara Planina and Kraishte. It lives semi-free in herds year round and is one of the smallest horses in the mod.

Almost always bay or brown. This is the most visually unified natural pool that ships: chestnut and black are each held at a fraction of a percent, present only as an admission that no one has shown either locus to be fixed.
Every dilution, every white pattern, grey and the leopard complex are forced wild. A primitive mountain landrace is not a licence to seed primitive-looking alleles that nobody has tested for.

Size follows the measured exterior study - a mean of 130.22 cm, inside a modern range of roughly 126-138 cm - rather than the older descriptions nearer 128 cm. The population is reported as taller and heavier than it was a century ago.
Cold tolerant near-fixed: it winters out in the mountains, which is the whole of its reputation, and health 10 is that plus foaling and thriving on thin grazing with no shelter.
Listed as critically endangered on Bulgaria's Red Data List of autochthonous domestic forms. By 2018 the four Rhodope rewilding herds together held more than eighty horses.
All disorders clear. No Karakachan carrier data was located, and hardiness is not evidence of immunity any more than rarity is evidence of disease.
The hoof quality, the herd behaviour, the pack and transhumance work, and the rewilding programme itself are none of them modelled.

name: Kentucky Mountain Saddle Horse
notes: An Appalachian gaited saddle horse out of eastern Kentucky, registered by the KMSHA since 1989. Its four-beat lateral single-foot replaces the trot entirely, and it is the everyday mountain riding horse the Rocky Mountain Horse is the famous cousin of.

Gaited near-fixed on DMRT3. The gait-keeper stop-gain is documented in the breed, and the locus ships even though the gait itself is still a roadmap item - the genotype is real whether or not the animation is.

The palette is wide and every bit of it must be solid. Bay, black, chestnut, brown, palomino, buckskin, dun, grey, roan and the silver chocolates all belong; the registry excludes bald faces, white above the knee or hock and any pinto expression, which go to the affiliated Spotted Mountain association instead. So every white-pattern locus is forced wild - a registry rule, not missing evidence.
Double cream is left reachable. The restriction is on white patterning, not on dilution, so a cremello founder is a legitimate outcome here.
Champagne sits at a token rate and is the weakest call in the file: it is real in the American gaited breeds generally and has no KMSH-specific count behind it. The draft itself offered to zero it.
Silver is deliberately below the chocolate-and-flaxen reputation of the Rocky Mountain Horse, which is a related but separate breed and should not lend it its public image.

The size band is the registry's own, and it is the widest in the mod: Class B begins just above 11 hands and Class A runs past 14.2 to something near 16. The two classes are registration categories over one gene pool, not strains, so the band spans both rather than splitting them.
All disorders clear. No KMSH carrier survey exists, and PSSM1 occurring across many horse populations is not a reason to assign this breed a founder rate for it.
Head nod, the single-foot itself, rider comfort and the KMSHA inspection are none of them modelled.

name: Kiger Mustang
notes: Strongly dun (dorsal stripe + leg bars) - the near-fixed dun does this. Some carry the leopard complex.
HERDA, GBED: both carried at the wild rate (PPIB, GBE1).

name: Kiso Horse
notes: The only indigenous horse breed of Honshu, from the Kiso district where southern Nagano meets eastern Gifu. A small, deep-bodied mountain packhorse, and one of Japan's eight native breeds.

This breed has a real coat survey behind it. A 2008-09 census of 125 horses - 86.2% of everything registered - found 105 bay, 11 dark bay, 5 buckskin dun and 4 chestnut, and no black at all. The pools are built to those counts rather than to the draft's own allele figures, which would have put chestnut at a tenth of the rate its own source recorded.
Black is not forced wild but is close to it: no black horse appeared in the census, so a/a sits at half a percent as an admission that a carrier pool is not the same as a fixed locus.

The dun pool is built backwards from two numbers, and it is the most deliberate thing in the file. A dorsal stripe was recorded on 66.4% of the census, while only 4% were classified as dun-diluted - so D is near absent and d1, non-dun with primitive marking, carries the stripes. Raising D to produce the stripe count would have painted two thirds of the breed with a body dilution nobody observed.

The 'buckskin dun' of the survey is read as dun, not as evidence that cream survives. Cream is forced wild, as are grey, silver, champagne, pearl, mushroom, flaxen, roan, the leopard complex and every white pattern.
Grey was in the breed in 1953 at 0.2% along with black, dark chestnut and palomino. The bottleneck took all four, and the modern population is what ships.

Managed sources only. There is no feral Kiso population - the surviving horses are a conservation herd, and a player who wants one should be buying it, which is also the way to run a breeding programme of their own.

Health 8, deliberately not higher. A breed rebuilt from a single surviving shrine stallion and his son, down to 32 horses in 1976 and near 149 registered in 2012, with a mean inbreeding coefficient of 0.11 and an effective population near 45.8, is a conservation concern - not a demonstration of exceptional robustness.
All disorders clear. The inbreeding is real and is not a carrier rate; inventing one from it would be inventing a disease.
Cold tolerant for Kiso winters. The thick winter coat, the hoof quality and the pack work are not modelled.

name: Kladruber
notes: The Starokladrubsky kun, the Old Kladruber - the oldest indigenous Czech breed and the baroque carriage horse of the Habsburg court, bred at the National Stud at Kladruby nad Labem since the sixteenth century. The stud landscape has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2019.

Two colours and nothing else, and they are two historically separate closed herds rather than one pool with two outcomes: the grey was the imperial and court horse, the black the ecclesiastical one, associated with Slatinany. That is exactly what a strain is for, and it is the only thing the strains differ in.

Grey is the only locus either strain names. The base is black at both - fixed E and fixed a - so a grey Kladruber is a black horse whitening with age, born dark and greying out, which is what the real ones do.

The 50/50 strain split is a gameplay reading, not the stud's roughly 250-grey-in-500 ratio, and the grey strain is near-fixed rather than truly fixed so that a grey pairing can still throw the occasional black.

Every other locus is forced wild. No bay, no chestnut, no dilution, no roan, no pinto, no leopard belongs in a pure founder, and the modern breeding programme is the reason rather than an absence of evidence.
One of the tallest breeds that ships. The band is the usual 16.0-17.0 hands, which puts its top on the Irish Draught's; wider figures from 15.3 to 17.3 are on record and are not what a founder rolls.
Managed sources only. Kladruby is a designed agricultural and training landscape, not wild range, and there has never been a feral Kladruber.
The black herd was dissolved in the 1930s and rebuilt; the reconstruction programme closed in 1973. Six grey and four black sire lines survive, and sire-line identity is not modelled.

All disorders clear. Research on the breed discusses melanoma and insect-bite hypersensitivity markers - melanoma being the standing risk of any grey population - but establishes no rate for any locus in the panel, so nothing was seeded.
The Roman nose, the baroque outline, the arched neck, the high knee action, collection, team driving and the whitening timeline itself are none of them modelled.

name: Knabstrupper
notes: ERU is age-related; folded into heartiness. CSNB on LP/LP is modelled (informational).

name: Konik
notes: The Konik polski - Poland's small native horse, out of the Panje horses of the Bilgoraj country, named in the 1920s and bred since 1955 in the continuous reserve herds at Popielno. It is the conservation grazer of European wetland and woodland rewilding, well beyond Poland.

One coat, fixed three ways: E_ aa D_ is blue dun, and every founder is a mouse grey horse with a dark dorsal stripe, dark lower legs, and a dark or dark-mixed mane and tail. Leg barring and shoulder shadowing come with the dun locus.

The shade pool is the only variation in the colour, and it is the right one - the standard runs from light mouse through dark mouse to a greyer dun, which is a depth difference rather than a different colour.

True grey is forced wild and that matters more here than usual: 'mouse grey' is a description of a dun, not a reason to seed STX17, which would whiten these horses with age and destroy the one thing the breed looks like.
Every white pattern is forced wild too. The pure-bred standard permits no white markings at all, with a narrow allowance for tiny temporary facial marks in mares.
This is the modern registered Konik polski, not the looser historical primitive Polish horse it came from, which is why the palette is closed rather than merely narrow.

Not a surviving Tarpan. The breed's own literature rejects that framing: it is a conserved domestic population with real bottlenecks behind it, and the resemblance is the result of selection, not descent.
Cold tolerant near-fixed. It winters out in reserve herds, which is the whole point of it, and health 9 is that thriftiness on poor wet grazing.
All disorders clear. No breed-specific carrier survey was found, which is a data decision and not a claim that real Koniks are disease-free.
The upright primitive mane, the head profile, the hoof quality, the seasonal coat and the wetland grazing behaviour are none of them modelled.

name: Lipizzan
notes: Born dark, greys to white; Roman nose, compact baroque build - head profile not modelled. Melanoma is age-related.

name: Lusitano
notes: Convex profile, sloping croup, baroque build - head/croup shape not modelled. OCD is age-related.

name: Mangalarga Marchador
notes: The Mangalarga Mineiro of Minas Gerais, registered by the ABCCMM out of Belo Horizonte since 1949 and one of the most numerous saddle breeds in Brazil. Iberian stock worked into a national riding horse over two centuries.

The marcha is the breed: a smooth four-beat amble with moments of triple support, ridden in place of the trot, batida diagonally coordinated and picada more lateral and usually called the smoother of the two. Gaited near-fixed on DMRT3 - the draft assumed the mod had no locus for it and it does.

Deliberately not a unified colour. Grey is conspicuous and common, bay, brown, black and chestnut are all well represented, and buckskin, palomino, dun, roan, sabino and tobiano turn up underneath. It should read as the most colourful founder pool in Latin America without every horse being a loud one.
None of these rates is a registry statistic. No population allele survey for the breed was found, and grey at something near a third of founders is the largest of the approximations.

Frame overo is forced wild on purpose. It is not documented in the breed, and seeding it would manufacture a lethal white cross where the real population has none - so a Marchador pair is safe to breed in a way an American Paint pair is not.
The leopard complex, champagne, silver, pearl and mushroom are forced wild for want of any evidence at all.
Heat tolerant heavily, for Minas Gerais.

All disorders clear, with the panel reasoned through: HYPP is a Quarter Horse Impressive-line disease, SCID, CA and LFS are Arabian, PLOD1 is Friesian, HERDA is Quarter Horse cutting lines. None of that ancestry is this breed's.
The marcha itself, gait timing, rider comfort, the three-year-old inspection, the mane-roaching tradition and regional bloodlines are none of them modelled.

name: Marwari
notes: Inward-curving (lyre-shaped) ear tips - NOT modelled (a mesh change, out of scope for now).
Sweet itch: age-related, folded into heartiness.

name: Medimurje Horse
notes: The Medimurje horse, properly Medimurski konj and also the Murinsulaner or Murakozi - a tall medium-heavy draught horse of the Mura and Drava lowland in northern Croatia. The name is written Medimurje with a crossed D that a breed id cannot carry.

Its landscape is genuinely transboundary - Croatia, Hungary, Slovenia and Austria all belong to it - and it is filed under Croatia because a breed is pinned to one nation here. The Croatian population is the smallest part of it: larger related herds survive north of the Mura in Hungary and in eastern Slovenia.

Bay and seal brown are the core, black is next, chestnut is less common, and the surviving Croatian animals include dark chestnuts and browns. The shade pool is skewed dark to carry the seal browns rather than giving agouti a second allele.

Its draft opened by arguing every founder should be black with agouti fixed recessive - and then corrected itself in the body, because that 'only black and grey' rule comes from a genomic study of the Italian Murgese, an unrelated breed that happens to abbreviate to MUR. The bay-dominant pool is the corrected reading. The actual Murgese ships in this same batch and is black-only for its own reasons.
Grey is real and rare. Every dilution and every white pattern is forced wild.

Managed sources only, and this is the rarest thing in the file: a 2018 systematization paper put the effective population near 14, with the Croatian source population around 40 animals. Microsatellite work found moderate diversity, low and non-significant inbreeding, and clear separation from both the Posavac and the Croatian Coldblood.
Health 8 rather than the draught-horse 9 or 10: a population this small is a conservation emergency, not a demonstration of vigour.
Lightly cold tolerant for Pannonian winters and lightly heat sensitive as the heavy breeds are.
All disorders clear. With a population this small, invented disease frequencies would be worse than usual - there is nothing to average against.
Traction, ploughing and logging skill, carriage training, mane density, feathering and the conservation registry are none of them modelled.

name: Misaki Horse
notes: The Misaki-uma of Cape Toi, in Kushima at the southern tip of Miyazaki on Kyushu - one of Japan's eight native breeds and the only one still living as a self-sustaining feral population. Local history dates it to 1697, when the Akizuki family gathered the district's horses, and the horses and their cape were designated a Natural Monument together in 1953.

The base pool reconstructs a Misaki-specific study of 99 horses: 79.2% bay, 12.9% black, 8.0% chestnut. The draft's own JSON figures do not produce those percentages and it says so outright - its corrected numbers are what ship.

Solid and dark. Face and leg white is very rare in the Japanese native breeds, and nothing supports grey, cream, dun, champagne, silver, roan, tobiano or the leopard complex in a pure founder, so all of them are forced wild.
No cowboy. This is an isolated conservation population on one headland, not sale-yard stock, so it is found in the wild or bought from a stable and never offered by a trader.

Wild is the point of it. A player should meet these on the coast, and the difference between a feral horse and an untamed domestic one is not something the mod models - so what makes them Misaki is the breed, not the behaviour.

The population bottomed out at 53 animals in 1973 and has recovered to something above a hundred. Health 8 carries that: a small, closed, unmanaged population is fragile, however hardy the individual horse.
All disorders clear. No Misaki carrier frequency was found for any locus in the panel.
Lightly heat tolerant for a subtropical coast.
The herd structure, the coastal grazing, the seasonal forage and the legal protection itself are none of them modelled.

name: Missouri Fox Trotter
notes: The saddle horse of the Ozark country of southern Missouri and northern Arkansas, organised at Ava in 1948 and the Missouri state horse since 2002. The fox trot is a broken four-beat diagonal - the front foot of a pair lands just before the opposite hind, one foot is always down, and the horse covers about ten miles an hour doing it all day.
Gaited near-fixed on DMRT3, alongside the flat-footed walk and canter the registry also requires.

The registry is colour-open and the pool is the widest natural palette that ships outside the Mustang: bay, brown, black, chestnut, palomino, buckskin, cremello, dun, grey, roan, champagne, tobiano, sabino and frame all belong. The rulebook has its own champagne classes - classic, amber, gold and ivory - which is the rare case of a registry naming the locus for us.
Frame is here at a real rate, so this is one of the breeds where two founders can produce a lethal white foal. That is the breed being what it is, not an oversight.
The leopard complex is forced wild: it is explicitly outside the documented range. Pearl, mushroom, dominant white and brindle have no support either.

Silver is at a modest rate and carries a caveat the draft raised and then got right: MCOA in this breed is a consequence of the silver PMEL variant, not a separate disorder locus, and PPIB is HERDA and belongs to Quarter Horse cutting lines. Neither was seeded as a disease.
All disorders clear. UC Davis offers a PSSM1 test in a Fox Trotter context, but the existence of a test is not a founder rate, so nothing was assigned.
Curly-coated Fox Trotters occur and there is no curly locus in the mod to give them. Curl is not required for breed identity here anyway.
The separate 11-to-14-hand pony registry is not modelled; the band is the documented 14-16-hand saddle horse.
The fox trot itself, the head nod, the sliding hind action and rider comfort are none of them modelled.

name: Mongolian Horse
notes: The steppe horse itself - a landrace rather than a studbook breed, a family of related local types with no single registry governing them, and by headcount one of the most numerous horse populations on earth.

There is no correct Mongolian coat. Bay, black, dun, chestnut, grey, roan and palomino all occur, dun and the dark bases are favoured across most of the country, and white horses carry a particular importance for the Darkhad. The pool is built to stay earth-toned and steppe-plausible: colourful, but not an Appaloosa herd and not an American gaited breed's champagne palette.
